accepted_claims.claim: Real-time VLA (Vision-Language-Action) inference for robotics targets a latency of 10 to 100 milliseconds (10 Hz to 100 Hz) to align with visual signal ingestion rates from standard RGB cameras (24-60 Hz).
accepted_claims.support: VLA-Perf analysis defines 10 Hz as a baseline and explores rates up to and beyond 100 Hz to match camera frame rates.

accepted_claims.claim: Diffusion-based VLA models are compute-intensive and often create a performance gap where the robot's 'brain' is too slow for its 'body,' resulting in motion jitter, stalling, and safety risks in dynamic environments.
accepted_claims.support: Multiple sources highlight the compute intensity of diffusion VLAs and the resulting 'performance wall' leading to stuttering movements.

accepted_claims.claim: The Deltoris framework accelerates diffusion-based VLA inference using a hardware-software co-design that employs temporal-aware bit-sparsity to compute only differences between consecutive inputs and speculative inference to amortize data loading.
accepted_claims.support: Deltoris uses customized 1D systolic bit-serial PE arrays to implement these techniques, achieving up to 34.2x speedup over mobile GPUs.

accepted_claims.claim: VLA-RAIL addresses VLA inference bottlenecks by implementing an asynchronous inference linker that uses a Trajectory Smoother (polynomial fitting) and a Chunk Fuser to ensure continuity in position, velocity, and acceleration.
accepted_claims.support: This framework decouples model inference from motion control to eliminate jitter and pauses in action execution.

accepted_claims.claim: Humanoid actuator energy efficiency is constrained by a trade-off between battery chemistries: Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) provides better thermal stability and cycle life, while Nickel Cobalt Aluminum (NCA) offers higher energy density.
accepted_claims.support: The choice of chemistry directly impacts the thermal budget and how aggressively the actuator stack can be pushed.

accepted_claims.claim: Rigid actuator systems (e.g., harmonic drives and brushless motors) are energy-inefficient because they require continuous power input to maintain position and generate force, whereas soft actuators can reduce power draw by passively storing and releasing energy.
accepted_claims.support: Soft actuators exploit material compliance to absorb and redirect energy, which is critical for power-constrained environments like planetary exploration.

sources.title: New Research: Robots Push Energy Limits in Three Different Directions
sources.excerpt: Rigid actuator systems, like the harmonic drives and brushless motors used in most humanoid robots, require continuous power input to hold position and generate force. Soft actuators can exploit material compliance to absorb and redirect energy more naturally.
sources.retrieved_title: New Research: Robots Push Energy Limits in Three Different Directions

accepted_claims.claim: Thermal management is a primary bottleneck for humanoid actuators in production; compact body designs constrain heat paths, leading to thermal throttling or faults during sustained operation.
accepted_claims.support: Actuators that perform well in labs may fail in warm environments due to constrained heat paths in the robot's body.
